Ukraine deployed drones to sink a Russian warship that had docked in Benghazi, a port in eastern Libya, where local forces have ties to Russia. A Russian cargo ship off Libya’s cost was also hit. Ukrainian drones had earlier attacked a Russian cargo vessel in the Baltic sea, which caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. Meanwhile, three Russian cruise missiles crossed into Polish territory and crashed. The Polish government accused Russia of a “provocation”, as military exercises were under way in the area at the time. In another sign of increased tensions in the region Russia described Estonia’s intention to close its border on December 1st as a hostile act that was “on the verge of triggering open war”.
German media reported that Russia was preparing to send a nuclear-armed satellite into space in order to destroy other satellites. The reports said the claims came from Western intelligence, though no specific agency was identified. Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor, said the reports were not new, but still shocking. He was speaking alongside Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, who reaffirmed that the alliance would defend “every inch” of its territory. The Kremlin dismissed the claims as propaganda for relying on unknown sources.
In Britain MI5, the domestic intelligence service, warned defence companies supplying military equipment or components to Ukraine that they could be targeted by Russia. Russia has increased its attempts to damage defence facilities in Europe, it said, which typically involves the use of proxy actors engaging in “low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson”.
At least 11 people were killed when a Russian drone hit a residential building in Dymer, about 45km (28 miles) outside Kyiv. Volodymyr Zelensky again urged America to send missiles for Patriot defence systems that have already been approved. The missiles’ delivery is being held up by Pete Hegseth, America’s secretary of war, according to reports.
The Houthis, Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen, continued their advance on the port of Aden. For the second time the Houthis struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s capital, which houses the sovereign-wealth fund. The rebels also claimed an attack on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest oil refinery.
Lawyers for Parastoo Ahmadi, an Iranian singer who in 2024 performed without wearing the mandatory hijab, said that she and members of her band and a producer have been flogged as punishment. Ms Ahmadi was convicted in June of “offending public decency” and was reportedly lashed 74 times.
Drone strikes killed four people in and around Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, and damaged buildings belonging to the UN. The Rapid Support Forces, which has been losing ground to the country’s army in the civil war, frequently attacks civilian targets with drones after it has lost on the battlefield.
A court in South Africa found that Cyril Ramaphosa, the president, had no case to answer regarding the theft of more than half a million dollars in cash from his private farm in 2020. The verdict overturns an independent report into the case and puts a stop to impeachment proceedings against Mr Ramaphosa. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Mexican soldiers captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores , also known as “El Chapo Isidro”, the head of the Los Mazatlecos drug gang in Sinaloa state. Mr Meza Flores had been on the FBI’s “Ten Most Wanted” list and America wants him extradited, but Mexico’s attorney-general suggested he would be tried in its own courts. Other members of the gang set off a wave of bloodshed in response to his arrest.
The UN’s annual climate talks ended without an agreement for the first time in 17 years. COP31, held in Antalya on Turkey’s southern coast, descended into fractious recriminations after the EU, Britain, Canada, Norway, Panama, Vanuatu and other least-developed countries refused to endorse a closing agreement because it did not mention phasing out fossil fuels. That phrasing was opposed by oil-producing countries, including Russia and Saudi Arabia, as well as India.
Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, said he had secured closer co-operation with the European Union in a number of areas. These include removing checks on food exports, a visa scheme for 18- to 31-year-olds and an arrangement on emissions trading that exempts British steel exports from EU carbon taxes. It was unclear whether the EU would agree to the terms without an accompanying deal to lower fees at British universities for EU students. Eurosceptics said Mr Burnham was making Britain poorer. He rejected criticisms that he wanted to return to the EU via the back door, saying it would be “unthinkable” to rejoin without a referendum.
China’s anti-corruption watchdog announced that it had placed the Communist Party’s chief in Shanghai under investigation. Chen Jining is also a member of the party’s Politburo, and is the fourth person from the powerful body to be investigated amid Xi Jinping’s purge on graft. Other members of the party leadership in Shanghai quickly convened to express their loyalty to Mr Xi and support for his crackdown.
The Solomon Islands signed a security pact with Australia. In a blow to China, the Pacific island state is reportedly set to ditch a similar but controversial agreement it had signed with Beijing in 2022. Australia has pledged to provide extra support for the Solomons’ education system, and funding for renewable energy and other infrastructure.
According to her spokesman, Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on December 16th, the country’s Victory Day marking the end of the war with Pakistan in 1971. The former prime minister fled to India in 2024 amid nationwide protests against her government. She has since been sentenced to death in absentia for ordering a brutal crackdown on the protesters. Bangladesh refuses to issue her a passport and warns that she will be arrested.
A Pakistani astronaut became the first foreign crew member to join China’s Tiangong ​space station. China is keen to promote its orbital lab, which has been operational since 2021, as the main hub for international collaboration. The NASA-led International Space Station is due to be retired in 2030, though Congress is considering expanding its life to 2032.

Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive, just two weeks after he resigned over his affairs with a suspected Chinese agent and, reportedly, two subordinates. The board had insisted that Mr Huang would not return, but Donald Trump intervened and pushed for his reappointment, arguing that he is essential to the AI industry. Some Republicans balked at Mr Huang’s return, claiming he had jeopardised American interests by sleeping with a woman who worked for a firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s chips to China. Mr Huang apologised to staff. “I made some terrible mistakes”, he said, adding that he is now in daily therapy.
Mr Huang’s return provided only a brief respite for Nvidia’s battered share price, and tech stocks in general. The NASDAQ 100 slid again, after registering its biggest one-week drop since the start of the pandemic, as investors increasingly question the financial fundamentals underlying the AI boom. Anthropic’s stock dipped below the $83 it had set at its IPO just a few days earlier (the share price had risen by 17% at the close of its first day of trading on November 19th).
Meanwhile, the Commerce Department announced that Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm widely suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s chips to China, would be barred from conducting trade with American companies.
A jury in New York found Huawei guilty of several criminal charges, including trying to steal trade secrets, but acquitted it of racketeering. Prosecutors had alleged that the Chinese maker of networking equipment was, in essence, a criminal organisation. The firm won’t be sentenced until September next year, giving it time to launch an appeal.
The American government proposed fresh tariffs on goods from 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, despite America having signed trade deals with these places. The administration said the countries were systematically overproducing goods for the world market. The new duties won’t come into force until January, allowing time for negotiations. In February the Supreme Court struck down most of Mr Trump’s previous country-specific tariffs. The administration thinks it is on firmer legal ground this time by utilising Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act.
One of the biggest-ever takeovers in the cyber-security industry got under way, as CrowdStrike announced an agreement to buy Zscaler for $44bn. CrowdStrike’s share price has soared this year as demand jumped for its Falcon platform, which protects computers and servers.
America’s national cyber director was sacked following a series of unconnected technological glitches that took down Microsoft’s communications platforms, bank websites and other services. The director advises the president on cyber-security issues.
American regulators gave permission for SpaceX to fly up to 1m Starmind orbiting data centres, on condition that the firm deploy its first satellite by November 2033, and 10% of the constellation by November 2035.
A Dutch court barred BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the EU, finding that the design replicates Jaguar Land Rover’s Defender. JLR, which brought the case, welcomed the ruling. The verdict is a blow to BYD’s ambitions to expand in Europe. The Chinese electric-carmaker insists that the Ti7 is its own design and does not infringe on JLR’s rights. It says it will “pursue every legal avenue” in an appeal. BYD nevertheless doubled down on its commitment to Europe by announcing talks to buy a production site in France.
Sanofi, a French pharmaceuticals company, embarked on its biggest acquisition in 20 years when it agreed to buy Insmed, an American biotech firm, for $41bn. Insmed specialises in treatments for respiratory ailments, making two popular drugs for lung diseases.
AI’s relentless advance into the field of mathematics continued. Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic, claimed to have solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis , which concerns the distribution of prime numbers. The task of proving it has defeated the world’s best human mathematicians since the mid-19th century. Working with Claude, Anthropic’s AI, Dr Alpöge used Lean , a programming language designed to verify the logical validity of mathematical proofs. Mathematicians are busy simplifying the proof’s 17m lines of Lean code to try and work out how the AI did it.
“Grand Theft Auto VI” took $3.8bn on just its first day of sales, a record for a video game , and indeed for any form of entertainment in any medium. By contrast “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, this year’s biggest film hit, has taken $2.5bn since its release in late July. The press reported an outbreak of “GTA flu”: workers and school pupils taking time off to play the game.

Humanoid Robots grip the imagination in a way chatbots cannot. So futurists have long been disappointed by humanity’s failure to build a real-life c-3po or Marvin the Paranoid Android. Large language models (llms) may have helped prove the Riemann hypothesis , a puzzle that had stumped mathematicians since 1859, but their cousins in the physical world still struggle to fold a bedsheet. The all-purpose flexibility and dexterity of the human body have been trickier to replicate than its intellectual output: the robots that have automated most of manufacturing are usually fixed-in-place machines that carry out the same task for ever. Those who fear the transformative effect of AI have taken comfort. Step away from screens, and the biggest impact of the technology in the physical world is dull-looking data centres.
All that, however, will soon change. As we report, general-purpose robots are getting better , fast. Engineers are applying the techniques behind llms to budding bicentennial men. Progress is rapid because robotics is starting to benefit from the same scaling laws that have, in four years, taken AI from struggling to count to the frontier of mathematics. By one metric, the capability of LLMs in the physical world, when hooked up to robots, is doubling every two months. Advanced AI may itself soon help develop better robotics tech. And hardware prices are cratering: the average price of one Chinese firm’s humanoid robots has dropped by 72% in two years.
So any story of how ai will change the economy is incomplete if it is not chock-full of general-purpose robots. They will come in all kinds of shapes, but it is humanoids that will be increasingly ready to perform any physical task a person can do. AI will bring the brains. LLMs have already solved the thorny question of how to communicate with robots (simply speaking to them does the trick) and of how they should map out a messy goal (LLMs excel at that). LLM-like models are improving, too, at the tougher task of steering androids reliably enough to navigate the real world. A robotic body will bring the accompanying brawn. As this potent combination proliferates, the implications for human work and life will be head-spinning.
The robot revolution will probably start in the home. The first million humanoids could hit American laundry rooms and kitchens within the next 5 to 15 years, forecasters reckon. Both are full of low-stakes chores that do not require robots to have so much strength that they are risky to humans. Unlike workplaces, where automation is often resisted and sometimes banned, few will protest against not having to load the dishwasher. Enthusiastic nerds will pave the way, as they already have with robotic vacuum cleaners and lawnmowers.
The liberation of humanity, and especially women, from domestic drudgery is no small blessing. The economic consequences will become truly profound in the years and decades that follow, though, as robots conquer factories, hospitals and construction sites. At a minimum, robots invert one of the laziest presumptions in today’s AI conversation: that only cognitive work will be disrupted. Desk jockeys hoping to retrain as builders, electricians or plumbers might be out of luck.
If there is no blue-collar refuge from AI, blunt government interventions like reserving specific classes of jobs for humans, as Bill Gates has proposed, will grow more tempting. A wider political backlash could also slow robots’ advance. Today, self-driving cars are spreading more slowly than the underlying technology permits, thanks to leery local officials and a rearguard fight by cab drivers, injury lawyers and others. Robots touch many more industries, so they could face more severe hostility—but probably not enough to stop them.
What would happen then? Where goods are made will change. Today free trade and comparative advantage mean that, as economies get richer and prevailing wages rise, factories move to where labour is cheaper. That could unwind if robots take over production, so that human wages no longer matter much. Land and energy prices, which depend a lot on policies and NIMBYism, will matter more. Voters may oppose robots less when it is foreigners’ jobs they are taking. If humans are no longer needed to pick fruit or lay bricks, governments may grow even less welcoming to migrant labourers.
The services economy could be upended. For hundreds of years many service jobs have proved all but impervious to productivity growth. String quartets, the economist William Baumol noted, demand as much human effort as they did in Mozart’s day. The same goes for jobs like caring for the elderly. Robots could break that pattern.
Relative prices and wages would then shift wildly. Many more goods and services would go the way of the T-shirt, as mass production makes them abundant. As has already happened in farming, output could soar even as prices collapse still faster, so that whole sectors all but vanish as a share of GDP. Not everything would get cheaper, though. Land and natural resources would remain scarce. Measured in terms of goods and services, they could become vastly more valuable. (If you thought rent was bad today, just wait until it forms most of measured economic output.)
Perhaps people will still be needed for management, steering, oversight and maintenance of robotic systems, just as tractors have not put all farmers out of work. Humans may prefer some jobs to be done by other humans—would a robot orchestra really be worth the ticket price? A preference for “relational goods” could allow humans to trade their labour for the goods and services robots produce. We hope so. An alternative is a highly unequal economy in which robots and AI work for those who own them, with everyone else competing with robots for energy, land and capital.
The past few years’ remarkable leaps in AI took the world by surprise. Today, most are equally unprepared for the prospect that a real-life c-3po could be around the corner. Time to get ready to meet him. ■

It took only 11 days for Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang , having accepted his resignation as CEO after he admitted to a series of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese agent. The company’s investigation into potential security breaches had barely begun. But Donald Trump called and demanded that his friend Mr Huang got his job back. It seems that Silicon Valley and America’s president share an imperial view of power and impunity. That should worry America —and the world.
Silicon Valley often idolises founders to the detriment of corporate governance. The veneration dates back to the triumphant return of Steve Jobs to Apple in the late 1990s, and has since been enshrined in the super-voting shares of the founders of Google, Meta and SpaceX. It operates even in cases where the founder lacks formal control. Take Sam Altman’s reinstatement as boss of OpenAI in 2023. Both he and Mr Huang prevailed over their boards, thanks in part to pressure from fellow Valley titans.
Brilliant founders can do extraordinary things. The euphoric reaction to Mr Huang’s return—Nvidia’s market capitalisation rose by $1trn, though it has since given up some of those gains—shows how much value investors ascribe to him, especially given Mr Trump’s assurances that he is not facing prosecution.
Yet unconstrained power can breed a recklessness that eventually damages companies and even countries. America shifted away from founder-controlled firms in the 20th century precisely to avoid these kinds of risks. For example, having built America’s biggest carmaker, Henry Ford ceded its dominance by refusing in the 1920s to update the Model T.
More recently Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly shrugged off complaints by Meta’s shareholders about his costly side-projects. He also stands accused of having ignored warnings by staff that his social-media platforms were poisoning public discourse and damaging the mental health of young people. On Mr Huang’s watch Nvidia is alleged to have turned a blind eye to China’s efforts to access its chips.
Unchecked power is even more dangerous in the hands of politicians. Mr Trump had several motives for intervening on behalf of Mr Huang. Fear that Nvidia would flounder without its long-serving boss, and bring the stock market crashing down with it, was one. “We have to protect our geniuses,” said the president, who happens to own shares in Nvidia. Moreover, he sees in the chip giant’s boss echoes of his own battles with critics. After Mr Huang’s return, the president posted online an altered version of the viral image of himself defiantly raising his fist while bleeding after an assassination attempt. In his place is Mr Huang—holding aloft a red bra. Mr Trump appears unchastened by his party’s defeat in the midterm elections and the mounting backlash against AI.
Congress must act. M any Republicans have joined Democrats in condemning Mr Huang’s reinstatement. They must now probe why Nvidia and the Commerce Department failed to control chip exports, and advance legislation to tighten the net. It beggars belief that Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary who allowed Nvidia’s chips to slip into Chinese hands, still has his job.
Shareholders may be pleased by the rebound in Nvidia’s shares. But in the long run they would be better served by a more competent board to act as a counterweight to Mr Huang and ensure a succession plan is in place. For all Mr Huang’s talents, his alignment with Mr Trump will make the firm a target for Democrats in Congress and, one day, the White House.
Mr Huang’s return sends a message: that the leaders of America’s most important companies will not be held accountable, so long as they enjoy the president’s favour. That undermines faith in the rule of law. It is no way to run an economy. ■

The TransWest Express transmission line is an epic feat of engineering. Designed to carry wind power from Wyoming to consumers in the south-west of America, it will cross four states, traversing mountains, deserts, canyons and rivers. But it is the line’s journey through American bureaucracy that is truly Homeric. In “The Odyssey” the obstacles were Cyclopes, Sirens and sorceresses; TransWest has had to overcome environmental assessments, inter-agency consultations and negotiations over permits. It took Odysseus a decade to return home to Ithaca. TransWest’s struggle to get all the permissions it needed lasted 15 years.
Such tales of builders battling red tape abound in America. High-voltage transmission projects take ten years on average to develop, permit and build, according to the Energy Department. In other industries, from manufacturing to mining, estimates suggest that permits alone take between two and nine years. At a time when America desperately needs new infrastructure, building things has become extraordinarily difficult. But a bill before Congress could change that.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) sounds like the sort of name politicians give a flawed bill to disguise its shortcomings. But the BAAJA would actually do a lot of good. It would streamline federal environmental reviews and impose deadlines on regulators. Approval processes tangled up across multiple agencies would be co-ordinated. And opponents seeking to delay or block projects would face new restrictions on legal challenges. The measure has already passed the Senate by 62 votes to 33.
But the provision restricting legal challenges has rankled green types. They worry that it will become harder to overturn inadequate environmental assessments, allowing damaging projects to proceed. Others on the left wonder what the rush is about. Come January, Democrats will control both the House of Representatives and the Senate, creating an opportunity to pass a bill more to their liking—one that leaves more environmental regulations intact. Only 14 Democrats voted for the BAAJA in the Senate, whereas 30 opposed it. Its fate in the House remains uncertain.
Democrats would be wise to re-evaluate their opposition to the bill. Start with the fact that America’s creaking air-traffic-control system is not the only bit of infrastructure badly in need of an upgrade. Roughly one in 15 of the country’s bridges are in poor condition, according to the Department of Transport. Around 40% of major roads are in poor or mediocre condition. A shortage of mines and processing facilities helps explain why America depends on net imports for more than half its consumption of 33 critical minerals. Its ageing electricity grid is struggling to accommodate new sources of power and to cope with booming demand from data centres.
Red tape does not just snarl the sorts of projects that liberals oppose, such as coal-fired power stations and oil pipelines. It also obstructs those they like, such as wind and solar farms and the power lines to connect them to the grid. Indeed, the BAAJA would probably wind up being positive for the climate, since more than three-quarters of the proposed generating capacity awaiting connection is wind or solar power. According to Rhodium Group, a research firm, the law could cut America’s annual greenhouse-gas emissions by as much as 148m tonnes, or 4%, by 2040. It also reckons that electricity would become cheaper and more reliable.
And what of the argument that Democrats might be able to pass a better bill once they are in charge? That discounts the legislative hurdles they will continue to face. To overcome a filibuster, at least four Republican senators would have to support any new legislation. And President Donald Trump would have to be willing to sign it—even though Democrats had rejected the BAAJA, a bill which he supports.
The Democratic Party faces a reckoning of sorts. It is torn between two competing instincts. On one side are those who have embraced the “abundance agenda” of building quickly to alleviate shortages of essential goods and infrastructure. On the other are progressives who distrust deregulation and dislike corporate power. Permit reform is a good test of which instinct will prevail. More than that, it is a test of whether the party that campaigned for the midterms on a platform of lowering costs—and won big as a result—can deliver tangible results.
The BAAJA may not be a perfect bill, but it is good enough. Both Republicans and Mr Trump support it. So should Democrats. No more delays. ■

By the end of the decade Britain’s government is set to spend 2.4% of GDP (£87bn or $114bn) a year on disability and incapacity benefits for people below pension age. In 2019-20 the figure was 1.4%. For a country with the highest borrowing costs in the G7, this jump in spending is a huge headache. The increase is about what the Treasury would pull in if it raised the basic rate of income tax by five pence in the pound. Put another way, the extra spending each year is what the Royal Navy needs to shell out between now and 2035 to ready its entire fleet for a future of uncrewed warfare at sea.
This sharp rise in disability payments is unusual by international standards, which makes it unlikely that the covid-19 pandemic is to blame. Rather than an epidemic of ill health, this is a policy failure: an unaffordable number of people are getting their hands on cash originally intended for the most disabled. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, says he is working “flat out” to get the benefits bill down “as quickly as possible”. But to turn pleasing rhetoric into action, Mr Burnham will have to decide whose payments are going to be cut. There is little sign that he is ready to make hard choices.
The Labour government has given two party bigwigs the task of rethinking welfare. On November 17th Alan Milburn, a former health secretary, published a review on getting more young people into work, education or training; 1m Britons aged between 16 and 24 are not doing any of these things. With luck Mr Milburn’s proposals will eventually cut the bill for unemployment benefits. But the projected savings are just £3.6bn a year by 2036. And helping youngsters make themselves useful will do little on its own to cut disability benefits, since these are mostly awarded regardless of income.
Hence the importance of a second report, by Sir Stephen Timms, the minister for disability, that was published on November 24th. He has been looking at “personal independence payments” (PIP), which are intended to help people cope with higher living costs caused by their ailments—such as bills for heating, taxis or specific foods. These payments can be worth up to £195 a week. Unfortunately, Sir Stephen did not suggest anything likely to arrest the spiralling costs of PIP. And although the Milburn review says 16- to 24-year-olds should be barred from claiming PIP, Mr Burnham has insisted that “no young person loses out from a cash point of view”.
If the prime minister wants Britain to have a sustainable welfare system, he must change tack. Taxpayers should continue to support the severely disabled, such as those who are paralysed. But the biggest share of PIP claims, at 39%, is for mental-health problems such as anxiety and depression. Since the main way to diagnose these is to ask people how they feel, and there are hefty cash rewards for saying you feel terrible, the incentives to game the system are clear.
To control Britain’s benefits bill, Mr Burnham should dramatically tighten the eligibility rules for PIP . One option is simply to exclude most mental-health conditions. Separate categories of benefit for the incapacitated and unemployed would still be available to those whose conditions render them unable to work. Another option would be for the government to follow New Zealand’s lead, and issue PIP-like benefits based on receipts detailing the actual costs claimants run up because of their ill health. The worst psychiatric disorders may impose monetary costs; feeling anxious or depressed largely does not. When surveyed by the Resolution Foundation, a think-tank, one in six claimants of PIP said they had incurred no extra costs as a result of their condition.
Getting measures like these past Labour’s backbench MPs might seem a tall order. None of them went into politics to play Scrooge with people’s benefits; they notoriously resisted welfare reforms put forward by Mr Burnham’s ineffectual predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. But Mr Burnham has banked plenty of political capital since coming to office in July, and if Labour balks at such changes, a future government will not. Conservative and Reform voters are itching to cut off payments to those they see as shirkers and spongers.
If Britain’s public finances deteriorate too far, bond investors could revolt and borrowing costs shoot up. In a crisis, that might prompt the government to cut all sorts of spending and to raise taxes in a hurry—with the worst pain borne by the least well-off. By restricting eligibility for PIP to the people most in need, Mr Burnham has the chance to get ahead of things, and make a creaking system fairer and more sustainable. ■

In the early 2000s many parents fretted about an epidemic of promiscuity among the young. Tom Wolfe, a novelist, wrote breathlessly about college hook-up culture. “It was in the air along with the nitrogen and the oxygen! The whole campus was humid with it!” Donna Freitas, an academic, warned of the alienating effects of casual sex. Conservatives and some feminists urged the young to slow down and think hard before throwing their clothes on the floor.
Mission accomplished. Young adults in rich countries are now having strikingly less sex than before. In just over a decade the proportion of 16- to 24-year-old British women who have never had sex has doubled, from 19% to 38%, according to new figures from National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), the flagship British sex survey. Among young men the rate jumped from 18% to 28% between 2010 and 2022-24. And although few places collect sex data as comprehensively as Britain does, it is clear that the sex slowdown affects other countries, too. In Japan, 55% of unmarried women aged 20-24 have never had sex, compared with less than 40% in 2005. In China the share of young women who said they had ever had casual sex fell from 17% in 2020 to 4% last year.
Older people are having less sex, too, and not just because they are older. In 2000 the median 35- to 44-year-old Brit had sex four times a month. In 2010 it was three times a month; by 2022 it had fallen to twice. Studies in America, Finland and France all show similar downward trends.
Part of the great slowdown reflects a decline in sex that one partner did not really want. In France, the share of women saying they sometimes or often do it only to please a mate, rather than out of their own desire, has fallen by about a sixth over roughly two decades. If women are growing more assertive, that is welcome. So, too, is a decline in teenage pregnancies.
But there is much more going on. Young people are taking longer than previous generations to become independent. When they are children, their parents hover over them and allow less unsupervised play. As teens, they are less likely to get part-time jobs or learn to drive. As young adults they are slower to leave home. In addition, covid-19 robbed many schoolchildren of opportunities to socialise in person with their peers, leaving them staring at screens instead of learning the give and take of healthy relationships.
To find a mate, you must go out and risk rejection, yet researchers worry that overprotective parenting has made the young more risk-averse. One study found that 36% of American college students were still being tracked on apps by their parents. Knowing that mum knows where you slept surely inhibits nocturnal adventures.
Helicopter parenting is not only oppressive for the young; it is also exhausting for parents. Young mothers in 2018 spent 52% more time looking after their children than mothers in the 1980s did. (Fathers doubled their parenting time, from a lower base.) Add this constant hovering to the burden of paid work and household chores, and it is hardly surprising that one of the most common reasons for couples with kids not having sex is that one or both of them are too tired.
This matters because sex does. Besides being one of life’s great pleasures, it is good for health (it can improve moods and reduce stress), for relationships (couples with unsatisfying sex lives are more likely to split up), and for general well-being. The slowdown among the young is especially worrying. Those who have not started by the age of 25 are less likely to enjoy happy sex lives later. So although the sex slowdown has complex causes, there is a strong argument for helicopter parents to relax a bit more, turn off all those tracking apps and give their offspring more freedom. ■

Bartleby’s evaluation of personalised pricing , by which new technologies enable retailers to tailor their prices to an individual shopper’s personal data, was nicely balanced (November 14th). But perhaps the most important danger of personalised pricing is that it would destroy the incentives towards innovation and productivity. The economy idealised by Adam Smith has many buyers and sellers, and prices are determined by an impersonal market mechanism. Hence retailers and other sellers are incentivised to improve quality and lower prices.
With personalised pricing the incentives change towards finding out as much as possible about customers in order to bamboozle them into buying goods or services, even when better or cheaper alternatives exist. So sellers focus on invading privacy, digital manipulation, and so on, instead of improving goods and services. Buyers are then incentivised to spend a lot of energy figuring how to outsmart the sellers’ methodology. This wastes resources and arouses justified feelings among consumers of being used.
Andrew OdlyzkoProfessor emeritusSchool of MathematicsUniversity of MinnesotaMinneapolis
Bartleby compared personalised pricing to eBay, where you reach a price based on your willingness to pay. But that’s an auction with a near-fixed supply of mostly non-substitutable goods. Personalised pricing is different from simply offering discounts to consumers who agree to share personal data. It means that data-engorged companies will charge consumers individually as much as possible. That is predatory behaviour.
Jonathan PooleCape Town
Markets work because prices carry shared information. Setting a price based on an individual’s traits removes that common reference point. The deeper problem is the cost of information. A seller spreads the fixed cost of data across millions of transactions; a buyer buys one ticket. That gap widens with every advance in AI. Airlines show how this plays out. Headline fares don’t show fees that surface later in the purchase, and buyers are profiled by device and location before they see a price. EVERY SO OFTEN, mathematics undergoes a revolution. The invention of calculus and the discovery of non-Euclidean geometry were both transformational. The discipline is currently being subjected to an even more forceful upheaval. The catalyst is the development of artificial-intelligence models capable of solving the most important mathematical problems. These tools are in many cases achieving a level of progress in weeks or months that previously might have taken decades, or even centuries.
The latest shock concerns the Riemann hypothesis, arguably mathematics’ most famous unsolved problem. Proposed in 1859, it describes a mysterious regularity governing the distribution of prime numbers. Generations of mathematicians have tried, and failed, to prove it. Now Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working with Anthropic’s Claude, claims to have succeeded. His proof, comprising 17m lines of computer code, has passed independent checks, though its wider mathematical scrutiny continues.
The implications are extraordinary. A problem that has defied the world’s finest minds for more than 160 years may have yielded to a collaboration between human ingenuity and machine intelligence.
It is tempting to regard all this with alarm. If machines can solve our most cherished problems, what is left for mathematicians? Such fears are understandable. But they overlook something fundamental about mathematics.
Mathematics is not a finite list of problems waiting to be crossed off a list. Every great advance has opened more doors than it has closed. Calculus did not exhaust mathematics; it created vast new territories. AI promises to do the same.
This prospect, both exhilarating and unsettling, has not come without warning. Within the past few months, Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been used to solve a dizzying array of foundational mathematical problems, ranging from how fluids flow to theoretical limitations on the speed at which certain computational algorithms can run. In most cases the solutions built heavily on existing knowledge, but combined ideas in ways that hadn’t been contemplated.
For a discipline that has long regarded original insight as the pinnacle of human intellectual achievement, this has been a profound shock. AI is changing how conjectures are formulated, proofs discovered and arguments verified. Formal automated proof assistants such as Lean can check mathematical reasoning with extraordinary rigour. AI systems can search vast landscapes of possible arguments, uncover unexpected connections and conduct mathematical experiments at unprecedented speed. Problems once considered impossibly laborious are becoming tractable. The boundaries between conjecture, computation and proof are shifting.
With AI’s help, researchers will tackle problems whose complexity previously placed them beyond reach. They will explore connections between distant fields, uncover structures hidden in enormous datasets and test conjectures on an unimaginable scale. The journey from a promising idea to a rigorous result could become dramatically shorter. Most excitingly, mathematics may become more ambitious. AI may make mathematicians, freed from more technical tasks, more creative, not less so.
But this new age will look very different from its predecessors. Its culture, and the qualities it rewards, will have to change. Mathematics has traditionally celebrated the individual genius: Newton, Euler, Gauss, Ramanujan, Mirzakhani. Even today, prestige attaches to the elegant proof and the solitary breakthrough. Papers commonly have only a few authors. That model may be approaching its limits.
In an AI-rich world, important results will emerge from collaborations involving researchers, software and computing infrastructure. Credit will be harder to assign. The distinction between proving something and understanding why it is true will become more important.
Mathematics is not merely a machine for producing correct statements. Its greatest achievements illuminate: they reveal unexpected simplicity and beauty beneath apparent complexity. Turning a computer-generated proof into a comprehensible explanation could become one of the most valuable forms of mathematical work.
The qualities mathematicians prize must therefore evolve. Asking fruitful questions, recognising significance, finding illuminating explanations and connecting discoveries to the wider world may matter more than technical virtuosity. Collaboration and the ability to work alongside intelligent machines will be essential.
Other sciences offer useful precedents. Astronomy was transformed when telescopes, satellites and digital detectors began generating more data than individual observers could analyse. Particle physics underwent an even more dramatic change. The discovery of the Higgs boson required formidable computing resources and thousands of scientists from around the world pursuing a common goal. Neither field lost its intellectual vitality.
Mathematics should follow their lead. It will need shared computational infrastructure, new conventions for allocating credit, strong verification procedures and institutions that support large-scale collaboration. Universities must rethink how mathematicians are trained and rewarded. Research funders should recognise that building reliable AI models can be as valuable as proving individual theorems. Above all, mathematicians must resist the temptation to judge the future by the romantic ideals of the past.
There will be regrettable consequences. Familiar skills such as an ability to complete lengthy, technically difficult calculations will become less valuable. Some longstanding ambitions will be fulfilled by machines rather than people. The experience of mathematical discovery itself will change. And in all of this we will need to be particularly mindful of the impact on the career development of early-stage researchers who are unsure how to prepare themselves for a future no one can confidently predict.
But scientific progress rarely preserves the culture that produced it. The question is no longer whether mathematicians can compete with machines. It is what they can discover together. The golden age of mathematics may be only just beginning. ■

FOR ALL the fevered talk about a “new Yalta”, few sensible observers expected much to be achieved at the trilateral summit on November 19th in Shenzhen between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. More important than the substance was the theatre of it all—especially for Mr Putin, keen to show he belongs at the superpowers’ high table, although in many respects, especially economic ones, Russia is an impostor. On one measure, however—nuclear weapons—it is China that is the laggard. And that explains why the summit did at least produce one clear result: the abject failure of Mr Trump’s ambition to kick-start three-way nuclear negotiations.
Mr Trump had arrived ready for such a move. But beyond a vague joint promise to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks”, he drew a blank. In practice, China will not join any such talks until it achieves parity with the other two. It is expanding its nuclear arsenal fast, but its readiness to negotiate will depend on more than just the size of its stockpile. By chasing the other two big nuclear powers, China is joining a different league, where nukes offer not just protection but coercive power.
For many years after it joined the nuclear club in 1964 China maintained a modest force of about 200 warheads. But since military reforms in 2016 its stock has grown steeply to the current estimate of 620 (see chart). That is less than half of what America and Russia each hold at readiness—numbers shaped by a cap agreed under the 2011 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START). However, both countries maintain over 3,000 warheads in storage bunkers; and the New START treaty expired last February. This puts China a long way behind.
Its first priority is to reach the number of about 1,780 weapons that both the other big nuclear powers hold at readiness. Catching up with the even bigger numbers kept in storage is a problem left to tomorrow. The Pentagon’s assessment is that China will pass the 1,000-mark by 2030, and reach its initial target in around 2035.
The fatness of these stockpiles is a consequence of three dimensions of cold-war thinking. First, mass—the sheer volume of destructive power. A nuclear superpower needs enough weapons to absorb a pre-emptive strike, and still be able to respond with overwhelming force. Second comes survivability, which requires diffuse methods for launching weapons. This is the so-called nuclear triad, involving ground options, offering volume; submarines hiding in the sea providing stealth; and aircraft bringing nimbleness and flexibility. That means a range of different weaponry, too. Smaller nukes for military targets (or demonstrations of force) and big ones for hitting launch sites and cities. The third dimension is posture: the readiness of the force, and the policies governing its use.
China has work to do on all three fronts. Expanding its inventory demands a lot of fissile material—the essential ingredient in a nuclear warhead. For the most potent types, China uses both plutonium and highly enriched uranium (HEU), to create a two-stage thermonuclear reaction. China’s current reserve, and the recipe for its weapons, are state secrets. But experts agree it does not have enough HEU (and barely enough plutonium) to reach a stockpile target of about 1,780. So China is busily enriching uranium—in amounts observed to have increased by 50% since the start of 2025, far more than its civilian-energy needs. This puts it well on track.
Balancing the nuclear triad is harder. The strongest leg for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is its ground-launched intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs). Since 2020 it has been expanding the number of underground silos from 20 to a target of at least 350—more than Russia has, and about four-fifths as many as America. The PLA is also improving the reach of its easy-to-hide truck-launched missiles. Its latest can threaten most of continental America. And the PLA’s rocket forces are anticipating national ambitions. Their total number of planned ground-launch options (550) exceeds the estimate of their currently available weapons (400).
At sea and in the air, things are less impressive. The PLA navy has only six ballistic-missile submarines—less than half the size of the Russian and American fleets—and a force of strategic bombers one-fifth the size. China’s subs are comparatively noisy and so detectable by acoustic sensors. This confines them to home waters, which limits their reach. But, probably thanks to Russia’s help, it is developing more capable replacements. With improved ICBMs, and ocean patrols, they could threaten not just Hawaii and Alaska but most of continental America.
Air operations are even more constrained. China has only one nuclear-capable variant in its bomber fleet, firing short-range ballistic missiles. Plans for a stealth bomber are up to a decade from fruition.
The PLA’s navy and air force are better equipped to threaten American military bases in the Pacific. China has designed the necessary lower-yield warheads for short-range ballistic missiles. Adding extra rungs to the ladder of nuclear escalation is a mark of maturing power.
But it is arguably in its nuclear posture that China has the most catching up to do. True nuclear-readiness—for example, the number of warheads routinely married to missiles, or nuclear-armed submarines on constant patrol—remains questionable. In a highly centralised, paranoid system, these things develop haltingly.

China’s new muscle is intended to deter American intervention in a conflict over Taiwan. Diplomats, business executives, investors and think-tankers flock to China. Typically, they tour a few ultra-modern automated factories, ride a high-speed train from Shanghai or Hangzhou to Beijing, eat sumptuous banquets at improbably large round tables and hold meetings with Chinese officials and bankers adept at sticking to turgid scripts.
Many leave impressed by the slick modernity of China’s wealthiest cities. The more intrepid also see some rougher edges. Invited to chat with several delegations, Chaguan heard one question again and again. Visitors wanted to know whether China’s social contract was in tatters. They assumed that for many years Chinese people had, in effect, traded away their political freedom for rising prosperity. With growth weakening, the jobs market in bad shape and property prices sharply down, they wondered whether that bargain was finished, and what might come next.
To Chinese ears, this question often sounds odd. The idea of a social contract, in Chinese translation, mainly evokes a book Jean-Jacques Rousseau published in 1762. It belongs more to Western political theory than to real life in China. However, a rich vein of discussion in China focuses on a related concept: how to earn political legitimacy and, by extension, how to squander it.
In the simplified version of the supposed Chinese social contract—the visitors’ version—the exchange is straightforward, even vulgar. You swap political rights for higher incomes. Legitimacy, by contrast, comes from multiple sources. The economy is one factor, with rising living standards produced as proof that the Communist Party is governing well. But it is about more than money. The party also delivers safe streets, good trains, gold medals at the Olympics and the promise of unification with Taiwan.
As Wang Qishan, a former vice-president, argued a decade ago, legitimacy is also derived from history. The party, it relentlessly reminds the public, ended China’s “century of humiliation” at the hands of foreigners with the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949 and has since presided over its rise to global superpower. There is a relative dimension, too. Other countries’ crises redound to the party’s benefit. A running joke about “Xinwen Lianbo”, China’s flagship nightly newscast, is that the half-hour programme can be divided into three ten-minute sections: the leaders are busy; the people are happy; foreign countries are in chaos. Protests in China? Those do not make the evening news. In America or France? Tune in for more.
But legitimacy is more than a tally of successes and failures. A newly translated book by a Chinese scholar offers a more rigorous approach. Zhao Dingxin of Zhejiang University breaks legitimacy into three parts. First, there is a procedural element, reflecting how leaders are selected. Multiparty democracy is often messy, far from an idealised Athenian state of affairs. But when delegates to the National People’s Congress voted 2,952 to zero to back Xi Jinping’s third term as president in 2023, it did not require quite the same involvement of citizens as, say, America’s recent midterms. So, procedurally, China starts with a legitimacy deficit.
Admirers of the Chinese system believe it more than makes up for this with an abundance of performance legitimacy. The country’s accomplishments—800m people climbing out of poverty, the world’s biggest high-speed rail network, the proliferation of dancing robots, to name a few—are taken as evidence that its governance is highly effective. Progress is objective and measurable. The trouble with performance legitimacy is that it is inherently unstable, as Mr Zhao puts it. The relationship between the state and the population becomes transactional, with people consistently wanting more. More wealth, better public services, a stronger army and so on. That is tough enough when the economy is strong—and much harder when it is weak.
Hence a turn to a third kind of legitimacy: ideological. In Mr Zhao’s view, this was the foundation of support for the party in the Maoist era. Many held the belief—inculcated in schools and mandated in struggle sessions—that China was on the right path. After Mao, as the economy surged ahead and corruption spread, the regime seemed to lose its moorings. Mr Xi’s mission, in part, has been to revive the importance of ideology. He has tried to restore faith in the party’s essence by, for example, promoting its “core socialist values”. In this, his chances look slim. Many in China today are too worldly and too practical to embrace the party as anything more than a vehicle for their ambitions. Another option is to unleash nationalism. Yet doing that is risky because it can generate demands—notably for immediate action on Taiwan—that go too far. A safer course is to build up China’s status as a superpower, back in its rightful place on the world stage. The parade of national leaders visiting China over the past year is, in that sense, pitched at a domestic audience as much as a global one.
Talk of legitimacy may seem tangential to the real basis of power in China. The party commands a suffocating security-and-surveillance system. Would-be dissidents have little chance against it. The party’s power rests less on the consent of the masses than on cohesion within the ruling elite. Why then make a fuss about legitimacy? Because it clearly matters to China’s leaders. Like Mr Trump and even Mr Putin, they crave public approbation. A sagging economy is a real challenge. Yet it does not mean that a simple contract between ruler and ruled has been voided. Instead, the party is emphasising other accomplishments and cultivating other sources of support. Its battle is not just material but spiritual. ■

HE DID NOT quite remove a shroud, roll away a rock and emerge from a cave, but Jensen Huang’s miraculous resurrection as Nvidia’s boss on November 22nd, eleven days after resigning from the post, triggered rapture among his acolytes in Silicon Valley. President Donald Trump, who intervened personally with Nvidia’s board of directors to get him back, posted an AI-generated photo of Mr Huang defiantly holding aloft a red bra, seemingly a reference to the sex-and-espionage scandal that felled him. Investors, too, have been euphoric, initially adding almost $1trn to Nvidia’s value (since pared back). But Mr Huang and his firm are still in serious political jeopardy, and American lawmakers are ready to haul them over the coals.
Mr Huang embodies one side in America’s debates about artificial intelligence. He is a champion of open-source AI models, which he and his supporters see as essential to counterbalancing the clout of proprietary model-makers like Anthropic and OpenAI. Mr Huang also fought against legal and regulatory efforts to restrict the sales of advanced chips to China, on the basis that it was better to keep Chinese firms on America’s tech stack and to encourage co-operation between the two countries. Proponents of his vision of AI cheered his return. “This is why America is the greatest country on earth,” enthused Gavin Baker, a partner at Atreides, a technology investment firm.
But if Mr Huang maintained a devoted following in Silicon Valley, his support in Washington has seemed to be dwindling in recent weeks. Marco Rubio, secretary of state and national security adviser, is said to have circulated intelligence showing that Alice Huang, Mr Huang’s mistress and a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm to which Nvidia had sold chips, had ties to China’s spy agency. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, publicly criticised Nvidia’s lax approach to Megaspeed under Mr Huang and urged tighter controls. On November 22nd Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, confirmed that the government was investigating Megaspeed and Ms Huang.
Mr Trump’s patronage seemed to overcome these hurdles. As stock markets wobbled in the aftermath of Mr Huang’s resignation, triggering fears of a deeper rout, tech bosses lobbied the White House to act. The president—working alongside J.D. Vance, the vice-president, who has long associations with the tech world—persuaded Nvidia’s board to reinstate Mr Huang, in part by telling them that Mr Huang’s hands were clean. “The United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security,” wrote Mr Trump on social media. “The attorney-general of the United States has confirmed that the US government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” When asked in an interview on CNBC whether he had assured the board that Mr Huang would not be prosecuted, Mr Trump replied: “We believe he’s fine.” Mr Clayton himself spoke to Nvidia’s board.
Michael Strain of the American Enterprise Institute, a think-tank, says that Mr Trump’s involvement is not necessarily unwarranted. “The government is well positioned to know the extent to which there’s a national-security concern here,” he argues. Nonetheless, Mr Trump’s decision to intercede with the board is also part of a larger pattern in the president’s management of the economy. He authorised Nvidia’s chip sales to China on condition that the government got a cut. His administration has taken equity stakes in 41 companies, including Intel, another chipmaker, according to a tracker by the Cato Institute, another think-tank.
Mr Huang now faces a bruising period. He is due to testify in front of a joint session of the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China committees on December 1st. That is just one of several probes, including a hearing by the Senate banking committee two days later, an inquiry by Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees and, some say, an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission into Nvidia’s accounting practices. At least eight Republican senators and as many House members have already demanded answers from the administration, with some expressing incredulity at the reinstatement. Critics include lawmakers close to Mr Trump, such as Senators Rick Scott, Kevin Cramer, Tim Scott and Pete Ricketts, and Brian Mast, a congressman. “The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire [Mr] Huang,” wrote Mr Cramer on social media.

Also on November 23rd the Commerce Department placed Megaspeed on its “entity list” of companies prohibited from being sold certain types of technology, having been criticised by Mr Bessent for failing to do so earlier. New controls on chip exports, chipmaking equipment and computing power are pending in a defence bill that has bipartisan backing. Support for that legislation was growing even before Mr Huang’s return. Now, notes Marc Short, a former chief of staff to Mike Pence, Mr Trump’s first vice-president, the president’s actions “may have invited a veto-proof majority enforcing export controls”. ■

American politicians have big goals. They want to beat China in the race for superintelligence. They want to green the electricity grid. And they want to revive domestic manufacturing, to name just a few. Realising these ambitions will require building lots of stuff, from data centres to transmission lines. But the enormous amount of red tape faced by developers means that just getting permission to start building is often a multi-year slog.
A bill trundling through Congress aims to change that by streamlining the permitting process for infrastructure projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) has passed the Senate and won the backing of Donald Trump, but its fate in the House of Representatives is uncertain. Many Democrats are opposed. For them, the bill could prove a test of their commitment to promoting growth and lowering prices, two of the party’s promises during the midterm campaign.
Most lawmakers agree that it is too hard to build things. According to estimates published in 2025 by McKinsey, a consultancy, securing federal permits for mining projects takes between eight and nine years, on average. For oil and gas pipelines the figure is six to seven years; for power generation, five to six; for transport infrastructure, four to five; and for manufacturing, two to three. No wonder, then, that America has built little high-speed rail or that expansion of the electricity grid is failing to keep pace with booming demand.
The BAAJA would make it easier to build infrastructure of all kinds, from mines that might reduce America’s dependence on China for critical minerals to factories that provide manufacturing jobs. It would do so by simplifying permitting procedures, imposing deadlines on regulators, improving co-ordination across agencies and limiting legal challenges that can hold up projects. In particular, it would take some of the sting out of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which mandates environmental reviews for projects involving federal land, funding or regulatory approval—and which many developers regard as the bane of their existence.
The most extensive reviews under NEPA typically take more than four years. The act allows opponents of a project to sue to stop it on the grounds that a review was insufficient. To pre-empt legal challenges, environmental assessments are exhaustive, often running to hundreds of pages. Still, lawsuits are common. One study found that roughly two-thirds of solar projects, half of pipeline projects and a third of wind projects requiring such reviews faced legal challenges. Even when opponents lose, litigation adds 18 months on average to a project. Under the BAAJA, courts’ ability to cancel a project solely because a review was inadequate would be restricted; there would be an opportunity to remedy the shortcomings first.
Many environmentalists oppose the BAAJA. Though they accept the need for permitting reform, they think the bill’s trade-offs—including an easier permitting regime for gas pipelines and weaker judicial oversight—are not worth it. Amanda Garcia of the Southern Environmental Law Centre, an advocacy group, says the BAAJA runs “completely contrary to what voters just told us in the election…which is that they want more input, more agency in decisions that are going to affect their everyday lives”. On a strategy call among green campaigners, a recording of which was leaked to Punchbowl News, one said that the bill “should not be judged just based on a net-emissions analysis”, but also on “ecological and community values”.
Such awkward positioning may reflect findings that the BAAJA would actually benefit the climate. Permitting bottlenecks disproportionately hinder clean power. Renewables make up the vast majority of projects awaiting connection to a congested grid. Modelling by the Centre for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), a think-tank, suggests that under the BAAJA 36% more wind, solar and battery-storage capacity would be added over the next decade than under today’s permitting regime. Waiting times would shrink (see chart 1). According to a separate study by Rhodium Group, a research firm, the bill could cut America’s annual greenhouse-gas emissions by as much as 148m tonnes, or 4%, in 2040 compared with their projected level.
The BAAJA also aims to make much-needed upgrades to the power grid easier. America actually has three main grids (or “interconnections”) and a patchwork of regional electricity markets. The operators of these systems do not talk to each other or plan their systems together, says Ashley Kang of Grid United, a developer of interregional transmission. The firm is building the North Plains Connector, a 420-mile high-voltage line between Montana and North Dakota. It will connect two grids, span three electricity markets and involve ten utilities. The firm had to approach each utility separately to get buy-in.
Under the BAAJA stakeholders would be brought together at the outset and the costs of long-distance lines allocated according to who benefits most. “Right now there’s no process,” says Ms Kang. The bill would also strengthen federal regulators’ power to override state authorities that seek to block transmission lines. Green types should be pleased by this, too. C2ES reckons the bill would more than double interregional transmission capacity, getting more clean electricity to consumers who live far from wind and solar farms.
By increasing the supply of electricity and obliging data centres to pay more than their fair share for grid upgrades, the bill should bring down prices. Residential electricity bills could be 3-4% lower in real terms in 2035 than under current policy, says Rhodium Group (see chart 2).
Democrats, then, must decide where their priorities lie. Many in the party have embraced the “abundance agenda”, or the notion that America needs to build more quickly to alleviate shortages and bring down costs. Others, though, look askance at deregulation. People close to the talks over the BAAJA are optimistic that enough Democrats will join Republicans in backing it. But even if the bill becomes law, the broader argument within the Democratic Party will be far from settled. ■

“MAiNLY, I just enjoy it,” says a firearms instructor in New Jersey, reflecting on the low recoil and reliability of his AR-15-style rifle. The gas-operated, magazine-fed semi-automatic is notorious because mass shooters have repeatedly taken advantage of its rapid rate of fire. That has led Connecticut and other left-leaning jurisdictions to ban the weapon. Yet at least 16m Americans own one, often choosing it for self-defence or sport.
The AR-15 is at the centre of a case up for argument at the Supreme Court on December 2nd. Khaya v Cook County asks whether outlawing the rifle violates the Second Amendment’s “right to keep and bear arms”. When, in 1994, Congress enacted a federal assault-weapons ban, the AR-15 accounted for about 2% of guns manufactured in America. But after that law expired in 2004 the rifle’s popularity rocketed and, by 2020, it represented about a quarter of the total. Public outrage over its use in mass-casualty shootings—including at an elementary school in Connecticut in 2012 and at a July 4th parade in Illinois a decade later—led to some state and local bans.
Eleven states have barred the sale and, in most cases, the possession of specific AR-style guns and of other firearms with certain features—pistol grips, telescoping stocks and flash suppressors that dampen the burst of light each shot produces. But gun owners find workarounds. The New Jersey instructor’s own rifle, he says, is “virtually identical” to a model his state bans by name—yet, with a few modifications, is perfectly legal. Given how ubiquitous and easily customised it is, attempting to ban specific models is like “trying to ban the internal combustion engine”.
Khaya turns on whether these rifles can be outlawed, not on whether the laws are perfectly drafted. But the ability to evade bans that target specific models and features shapes both sides’ arguments. Challengers say the prohibited features are largely cosmetic and do little to make the guns more dangerous; the states reply that the restrictions leave plenty of alternative guns suitable for sport and self-defence. Joseph Blocher, a law professor at Duke University, acknowledges that barring certain features may seem silly—but so does claiming a Second Amendment “right to scary-looking features”.
The justices’ decision will draw upon a series of recent precedents. The first touchpoint is District of Columbia v Heller, the landmark case from 2008 that protects an individual’s right to keep a handgun at home for self-defence. Heller covers weapons that are “in common use”, but allows lawmakers to ban “dangerous and unusual” weapons—including the M-16, the fully automatic cousin of the AR-15.
In 2022 the Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority adopted a strict new regime for judging the constitutionality of gun laws: only laws consistent with America’s “historical tradition of firearm regulation” could survive. Two years later the court ruled 8-1 that a domestic abuser could be stripped of his weapons without violating his right to bear arms. A law needs only to be “consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition”, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote.
The AR-15’s advocates, backed by the Trump administration, say Heller settles the matter: the rifle is plainly “in common use”. Yet Elizabeth Prelogar, who successfully argued the domestic-abuser case, points out that lawmakers in medieval England and 19th-century America banned popular but dangerous weapons such as slingshots, lancegays and Bowie knives.
AR-15s, for all their firepower, are not machine-guns: each shot requires a separate pull of the trigger. Yet it may prove tricky for the court’s conservative majority to craft a decision that extends constitutional protection to semi-automatic rifles alone. Nearly 200,000 fully automatic machine-guns, registered before a law froze new registrations in 1986, are legally owned. Though Mr Blocher says he would be “genuinely stunned” if the Supreme Court expanded the Second Amendment to embrace military-grade weapons, that “is where the logic would point”. ■

A decade ago, despite receiving nearly 3m fewer votes than his opponent, Donald Trump became president thanks to the electoral college. Among the states that powered him to victory were Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In the recent midterm elections, Democrats secured trifectas in all four—meaning they will control both chambers of the state legislature and the governor’s mansion. Now they have a chance to turn the electoral college on its head. Eighteen states have adopted the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, pledging to award their electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote. The agreement will take effect only when its members collectively command a majority of electoral votes. If Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin joined, the compact would cross the threshold, potentially transforming presidential elections.
With new majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate, Democrats are hoping to transform a good many things. But in Washington they will continue to face vetoes and filibusters. It is in the states that the party might really assert itself. The midterms produced six new Democratic trifectas, bringing the party’s total to 22. Over half of Americans will soon live in states fully controlled by Democrats and more than two-thirds will have a Democratic governor. With state power comes enormous sway over everything from education to health care. How might the Democrats use it?
Common priorities are emerging across the states. New Democratic governors have promised to curb data-centre construction. In Nevada Democrats could repeal the state’s “right-to-work” law, which prevents unions from requiring workers to contribute to the cost of collective bargaining. Similarly, Wisconsin could roll back restrictions on public-sector unions. Minimum-wage increases are on the agenda in several states. Arizona Democrats could seek to repeal abortion restrictions. And in states such as Texas and Georgia, new Democratic attorneys-general will probably take a less aggressive approach to enforcing and defending abortion bans.
But Democrats will struggle to reverse some Republican policies, even where they campaigned explicitly against them. Take school vouchers, which give parents public money to spend on private education. In Iowa and Texas the schemes have proved divisive, not least among rural Republicans who fear for the future of public schools in communities with few private alternatives. Rob Sand, Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect, called his state’s programme a “siphon of hundreds of millions of dollars away from public schools”. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect of Texas (pictured), said in her victory speech that she would “work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas vouchers scam”.
Repealing the programmes will be tricky, though. To get them through their statehouses, Kim Reynolds and Greg Abbott, the outgoing Republican governors of Iowa and Texas, helped defeat rural Republican opponents in legislative primaries. Mr Sand and Ms Hinojosa must now work with some of the lawmakers who replaced them. Iowa has a Republican-controlled House and Senate; Texas has a Republican-controlled Senate. More modest reforms may be the most achievable outcome. Even in Arizona, where Democrats secured a trifecta, the state’s voucher scheme seems likely to survive.
Health care is another area where Democrats made big promises, but their ambitions may be frustrated. In Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin, newly elected Democratic governors vowed to expand Medicaid, the health programme for the poor, through the Affordable Care Act. Under the law the federal government picks up the tab for 90% of the cost of covering newly eligible adults, a financial incentive that has persuaded 40 states to expand the programme since 2014.
The difficulty is that Republicans still control at least one legislative chamber in most states that have resisted expansion. And Mr Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill”, passed last year, has made expansion less of a bargain. It eliminated an additional financial incentive for states that had yet to expand Medicaid, and obliges states to impose work requirements on recipients starting in 2027. That means spending millions of dollars on new staff and technology. The administration recently offered states an optional six-month reprieve from enforcing the requirements.
This points to a broader challenge for Democrats. Most states are in reasonably sound financial shape, helped in recent years by federal largesse and surging tax revenues. But revenue growth is slowing just as federal cuts to Medicaid, food assistance and other programmes are placing additional pressure on budgets. That will make it harder for Democrats to keep promises aimed at bringing down the high cost of living, such as subsidised child care and property-tax relief. Ms Hinojosa pledged to send a one-off $1,500 cheque to every household in Texas. The scheme would cost some $17bn.
The midterms gave voice to an angry electorate seeking big changes. Democrats captured that energy with ambitious agendas. Will voters tolerate the trade-offs and compromises that are a natural part of governing? Repealing school-voucher programmes and expanding Medicaid may prove just as difficult as changing how America elects its presidents—perhaps more so. Winning power seemed like the hard part for Democrats. Using it may prove the greater challenge. ■

There were snacks (potato chips), juice breaks (a coffee bar) and recess (cocktail hour). The gathering, put on by the National Governors Association (NGA), is technically called the “New Governors Leadership Forum”. But among existing governors, who act as faculty, it is known as “baby governor school”.
In recent years the NGA’s allegiance to a bygone bipartisanship has brought it to the brink of irrelevance. Some states stopped paying dues; others shirked meetings. President Donald Trump undermined it by trying to bar governors he disliked from White House meetings. But this year’s baby governor school marked something of a comeback. Of the new state governors elected in the midterms, 16 of 21 schlepped to Park City—representing states from Alaska to Maine. What did they learn?
Courses on offer included “Building your first budget”, “When disaster strikes” and “Family, privacy and the public eye”. Current and former governors offered sage advice such as “Don’t get into stupid lawsuits”.
“Baby governor school” was not a universally adored phrase. Phil Weiser of Colorado preferred “governor’s orientation”. Byron Donalds of Florida was quick to remind your correspondent of his work in Congress. At times, he says, he found himself thinking “Yeah, I know that already.” Other new governors shrugged off the hazing. “I’ve never been a governor before!” acknowledged Deb Haaland of New Mexico, a former congresswoman and cabinet secretary.
Final exams were on-stage interviews at the Politico Pub, a hotel ballroom the news outlet tried to infuse with ambience. Most new governors, showing their mastery of the non-answer, waffled when asked who might run for president in 2028.
