MexicAN officials are celebrating a win. On the evening of November 20th the country’s soldiers collared a powerful drug lord in the north of Sinaloa, a violence-ridden state. Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was captured during a raid on his house in the town of Guasave. The operation used Black Hawk helicopter gunships and 361 people; four soldiers were killed during the action. That is a reflection of just how much firepower Mexico’s gangs wield.
Mr Meza Flores is the boss of a group allied with a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, one of Mexico’s big two gangs. The FBI had him on its “Ten Most Wanted” list, and had offered up to $5m for information leading to his capture. American prosecutors accuse him of flooding the United States with drugs, including fentanyl. No one will regret seeing El Chapo Isidro in a cage—but his arrest could beget more violence, at least for a while. After the operation gunmen loyal to him blocked streets and burned vehicles. The men he commanded could fight each other for supremacy, causing turmoil in a bit of Sinaloa that had been relatively peaceful.
Mexican officials have long had to balance their desire to bag bad guys against a pragmatic wish to keep the peace. On this occasion, their calculations were doubtless influenced by a desire to placate Donald Trump. He talks a lot about sending troops over the border. He often says, falsely, that gangs run Mexico (most recently on the day Mr Meza Flores was captured).
President Claudia Sheinbaum’s strategy towards her capricious counterpart has been to co-operate, but also to seize opportunities to prove Mexican forces can pull off complex operations alone. As with the killing in February of Nemesio Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, the head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, only Mexican soldiers were on the ground for the latest raid. But the United States provided intelligence: a US surveillance drone helped pinpoint the gangster’s house.
The arrest may look to some like progress, but with demand for drugs unchanged, it will alter little. Two years ago another kingpin, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada García (a co-founder of the Sinaloa Cartel) was captured and flown to the United States. It sparked a horrific war between two Sinaloa factions for control of the business. Gang members roamed the streets of Culiacán, the state capital, in convoys. The state’s murder rate doubled in 2025 (see chart).
Sinaloa is a test for the anti-gang strategy that is evolving under Ms Sheinbaum and her popular security minister, Omar García Harfuch. They have broken from the hands-off approach employed by Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Ms Sheinbaum’s predecessor and mentor, which permitted gangs to grow. The Mexican army now has over 22,000 soldiers in Sinaloa, accounting for around a quarter of all soldiers deployed for public-security tasks across the country’s 32 states.
The government says Sinaloa is safer than when its current gang war first erupted. True, armed convoys no longer bear criminals through the streets. Murders in Sinaloa fell by 43% between June 2025, the deadliest month of the war when 207 people were killed, and June 2026, when 118 were. But lately the gains have stalled. Last month 169 people were murdered in the state: 39 more than in October 2025.
Moreover, the violence has moved location—including from the cities to rural areas—and transformed in type, says David Mora of International Crisis Group, a think-tank based in Brussels. Sinaloans are now terrorised by drone-delivered explosives and landmines. The troubles in the state were left unchecked for too long, reckons Natalia Luna Cárdenas, a 24-year-old graphic designer who lives in Culiacán. By the time you “see a few insects, the walls are already infested”, she says. Yet the violence often appears to fluctuate in patterns that don’t seem much related to anything the government does.

If an infusion of money has fixed the original complaint, any further funding is wasted. HUMANS NEED salt. It contains sodium, which helps regulate the body’s fluid balance; enables muscles to contract and relax; and helps the intestines absorb nutrients. It also adds flavour to even the blandest of dishes. But one can have too much of a good thing. Sodium raises blood pressure and excessive consumption is linked to cardiovascular and kidney diseases. Some manufacturers say certain varieties mitigate the harm. Are they right? Or should such claims be taken with a pinch of the proverbial?
Despite their differing appearances and price points, most supermarket salts—from fleur de sel to pink Himalayan—predominantly consist of plain old sodium chloride. Although some contain trace amounts of other minerals, such as calcium, iron and zinc, there is little evidence these make them any healthier. A study published in Foods in 2020, for example, analysed the mineral composition of pink salts available in Australia, including those of Himalayan origin. The researchers found that the mineral concentrations were so small that one would need to consume over 30g per day to make a difference, six times the WHO’s recommended daily limit.
Only two additives are worth their salt. The first is iodine. This chemical plays an important role in the healthy development of brains as well as bodies. The consequences of a deficiency can be severe, particularly among growing children and pregnant women. Iodine has many sources, such as milk, eggs and fish, and many will get enough from their usual diet. But iodised salt is a cheap and effective way to boost one’s intake.
The second is potassium. In order to minimise how much sodium salt contains, food scientists have long experimented with replacing some of the element with the closely related potassium. Matthew Bailey, a physiologist at the University of Edinburgh, describes the stuff as a “double whammy”: too little potassium, like too much sodium, pushes blood pressure up. Potassium-enriched salts therefore tackle two birds with one stone, and do so without altering taste or texture.

Those with kidney disease should beware: too much potassium can cause complications. For everyone else, though, the benefits are clear. ■

Hers was no ordinary nose. She was hyperosmic, meaning she had a hugely heightened sense of smell: acute enough to tell brands of tomato juice at a sniff, and to relish the wood-spice notes of childhood Crayola crayons. She put it all down to the fact that her mother’s waters had broken right at the perfume counter in Wanamaker’s; her baby genes probably got scrambled then, and smell, the weakest sense, emerged on top. She spent her career building on that. As a result America’s perfume industry, worth about $500,000 in 1962, was worth, six decades later, $62bn, a third of it accounted for by men.
The problem, she quickly saw, was the word “perfume” itself. When she was growing up it usually meant one pretty bottle on the dressing table, given by a partner. It was special, for Saturday nights, when non-working women doffed their aprons for a black dress, permed hair, a little string of pearls, and went out smelling nice for their companion. Then the bottle went back till the next week. No wonder, given this pace of use, that the Fragrance Foundation—set up in 1949 by six leading houses to educate Americans about perfume—was on its knees by 1962, and in desperation asked her to come and run it. She did so for 40 years.
Her résumé was mostly journalism on Hearst magazines, focusing on fashion and beauty. But she was good at PR, and her plan was simple: to start a revolution. It took ten years, because she had to start by educating the American pharma companies that had now bought up many of the old French houses. The first step was to replace the staid “perfume” with “fragrance”, lighter, more playful and in many cases cheaper, like colognes. It was not something to be coveted, bought and flaunted, like a car or a scarf; it was an emotional impulse-buy that reflected an inner mood, and moods changed often.
This meant there could be fragrances for different times of day. Spearmint, or a spicy, fresh botanical was good for morning; cinnamon to spur screen-tasks or shopping at midday, when most fragrance-buyers were now at work; lavender for cosy evenings back home. Her own regime was to change her perfume three or four times a day. She recommended a Wardrobe of Fragrance, to be varied as frequently as clothes. That might mean dozens of bottles on every flat surface, as there were on hers, but why not? They were beautiful and fun. Fragrance should be worn not just to please a partner, but to please yourself. Spritz on a wrist, new you.
As the idea caught on, sales soared. In 1973 she brought in the FiFi awards for the best “noses” and the best new fragrances, explicitly modelling their glitz on the Oscars. Alongside those came annual “Fragrance Weeks”, when retailers went all-out to lure new customers and increase “odour-awareness”, first in New York but then, on eager demand, nationwide. Her memoir was entitled, proudly, “Spritzing to Success”.
The enterprise also had a more academic side. She set up a Sense of Smell Institute and started seminars at the Fragrance Foundation by neuropathologists, clinical psychologists, anthropologists, futurists, even city planners. The psychological effects of both good and bad smells could be so overwhelming that they needed study. A report by the Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre found, for example, that 62% of patients going for CT or MRI scans were soothed when essence of vanilla was piped into the ward. Why did this happen, and how could fragrances be developed to enhance these effects? As a businesswoman, she needed to know.
The fragrance industry also had to be socially aware. Hence the futurologists at her seminars. In the late 1960s and 1970s, surprisingly, a craze for musk had erupted. Hippies started it. Musk was heavy, cloying and useful to hide the smell of pot, but it went mainstream fast, and the industry was late adjusting. “Oriental” perfumes, (patchouli, jasmine) followed. She stayed alert after that to fashions arising from the streets, or because habits changed. Would people who worked from home bother to switch fragrances as often as she recommended? Perhaps not. But would a digital, computerised world increasingly long for that soft, alluring touch? Probably yes. By the 1990s people seemed to be keener on perfume than at any time in history—or at least, she estimated, since Louis XV.
There remained the environment to think about. She did her best to improve that, too. She lobbied City Hall to wash and deodorise the garbage trucks each week, encourage the planting of scented window boxes and pipe nice smells into the subway. None of that happened, predictably. In Fragrance Weeks she gave the city a taste of what she would do if she were mayor, filling fountains with perfume and hanging flowers round the lions outside the main branch of the New York Public Library.
She never created a perfume herself. (Nor did she have a favourite, though Jean Patou’s “Joy” sprang easily to her mind.) But one, “Annette’s Greenhouse”, was created for her by Frank Voelkl, a master-nose, in her tenth decade. It was light, slightly spicy, cucumbery and very green. To wear it outside was the coolest possible antidote to whatever else might waft her way. ■
